html:
One of the oldest surviving Christian icons, painted in the 6th century and kept at Saint Catherine's Monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai in Egypt. It is the earliest known picture of Christ as Pantocrator, "ruler of all".

It is painted in hot coloured wax on wood, a technique called encaustic that goes back to Egyptian mummy portraits. Christ holds a jewelled book of the Gospels and blesses with his right hand. The two halves of his face differ in look and mood, which many read as showing his divine and human natures, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon. It was probably made in Constantinople, perhaps as a gift from Justinian, who founded the monastery.

It survived because Sinai fell to the Arab conquests in the 7th century. The Byzantine emperors who ordered images destroyed during Iconoclasm had no power there. It was cleaned of later overpainting in 1962.
sum: One of the oldest surviving Christian icons, painted in the 6th century and kept at Saint Catherine's Monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai in Egypt. It is the earliest known picture of Christ as Pantocrator, "ruler of all".
